walkthroughs.body_html:
International Trade and the Global Economy — a core area of GCSE Economics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

International Trade and the Global Economy brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with International Trade and the Global Economy.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Specialisation based on lowest opportunity cost is:
options: Absolute advantage
Comparative advantage
Free trade
Protectionism

mcqs.q: A tariff is a tax on:
options: Exports
Imports
Domestic production
Consumption

Consumer surplus is leftover stock that consumers haven't bought yet.
Consumer surplus is the profit that consumers make.
The difference between what consumers are willing to pay and what they actually pay — represented by the area below the demand curve and above the price line.
Marginal cost is the total cost of producing all units.
Asymmetric information is when a market only operates in one direction.
The change from one additional unit — marginal cost is the cost of producing one more unit; marginal utility is the satisfaction from one more unit. Marginal is incremental, not total or average.
Marginal means unimportant or small.

mcqs.q: What is asymmetric information as a source of market failure?
options: Asymmetric information means a buyer and seller disagree about a price.
Asymmetric information is when a market only operates in one direction.
Consumer surplus is the profit that consumers make.

When one party in a transaction knows more than the other — leading to problems like adverse selection (used-car market) or moral hazard (insurance). Markets can fail or unravel when information is unequal.
